sentences.text: The genus Kritosaurus was formally named by the paleontologist Barnum Brown in the year 1910.
The type specimen, which serves as the basis for the species description, includes a partial skull, lower jaws, and connected body bones, featuring a distinctive wide tip on the snout.
Although the name is sometimes mistakenly thought to mean noble lizard, it actually refers to a specific profile shape in the original restoration.
This animal is classified as a hadrosaurine, a subgroup of duckbilled dinosaurs known for having flat or solid crests on their heads.
A partial skeleton discovered in Mexico reaches a length of 11 meters, making it one of the largest well-documented North American saurolophines.
The type species, Kritosaurus navajovius, measured approximately 10 meters long and weighed around 4 tons.
Another specimen found in Sabinas, Coahuila, measures between 11 and 12 meters, exceeding the size of the type species.
Barnum Brown located the original type specimen, cataloged as AMNH 5799, near Ojo Alamo in San Juan County, New Mexico, in 1904.
By 1916, Brown determined that the fossils belonged to the late Campanian-age De-na-zin Member of the Kirtland Formation.
Brown also described an unnamed species of Kritosaurus, likely Kritosaurus navajovius, from rocks in the Ojo Alamo, Javelina, and El Picacho formations starting in the 1930s.
Kritosaurus was a large herbivore that moved on two or four legs and used its complex skull to grind plants in a chewing-like motion.
Its mouth contained dental batteries with hundreds of teeth, ensuring that only a few were active at any specific moment.
These teeth were constantly replaced, packed tightly within the dental batteries to maintain a functional set.
The animal used a toothless, horny beak at the front of its mouth to grasp vegetation, which was held in place by a skin structure acting like cheeks.
Its diet included vegetation ranging from the ground up to heights of about 4 meters.
Fossil evidence suggests Kritosaurus fed on plants reaching up to four meters in height.
This large herbivore alternated between bipedal and quadrupedal stances while processing food with its sophisticated skull.
Researchers propose that the nasal crest served social purposes, such as identifying sexes, species, and social rank.
It is hypothesized that inflatable air sacs flanked the crest to aid in visual and auditory signaling.
The nasal crest, whose true form remains unknown, may have been used for sex identification, species recognition, and social grading.
The crest might have consisted of inflatable air sacs on either side for communication through sight and sound.
Barnum Brown later synonymized the genus Gryposaurus with Kritosaurus, a decision supported by Charles Gilmore.
In 1984, José Bonaparte and colleagues named Kritosaurus australis based on fossils from the Los Alamitos Formation in Patagonia, Argentina.
The name Anasazisaurus is derived from the Anasazi people and the Greek word for lizard, though this is a separate taxon.
A partial skeleton from the Sabinas Basin in Mexico was initially described as Kritosaurus sp. but was later considered an indeterminate saurolophine.
Kritosaurus lived approximately 74.5 to 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period in North America.
Fossils of this dinosaur have also been found in the Olmos Formation in Mexico.
The habitat of Kritosaurus was interpreted as river floodplains that formed after the retreat of the Western Interior Seaway.
Kritosaurus lived at the end of the Cretaceous Period, approximately 73 million years ago during the Campanian, in what is now North America.
It is debated whether Kritosaurus is a valid genus, as some researchers judged it a nomen dubium due to a lack of diagnostic features.
There is a debate regarding the age of the Kritosaurus holotype because the Ojo Alamo Formation is divided by an unconformity into older Campanian and younger Maastrichtian members.
